synopsis: Oceania. The Ministry of Truth. Big Brother watches. You buy a diary on impulse. Today you write: down with Big Brother.

nodes.text: The alcove is the one corner of the flat the telescreen cannot quite reach — a builder's oversight thirty years old that has probably killed people. The book is cream-laid paper from before the Revolution, bought in the prole quarter for a fortnight of not eating properly. The nib catches on the surface. Your hands are the only part of you out of shot. Ink is a confession you cannot take back.

choices.consequence: You write it six times in capitals and your bowels turn to water, and the day the Thought Police come for you is now fixed, whenever it happens to fall.
You put down the date instead — April the fourth, you think, though nobody is certain of the year any more — and the cowardice tastes exactly like the gin.

nodes.text: Six-thirty. Physical Jerks. The instructress barks from the screen at a woman she can apparently see and you certainly cannot. Your face has to hold the correct expression while your body performs the touching of toes. There is a word here for wearing the wrong face and it carries five years: facecrime. The ulcer above your ankle itches under the sock. You do not scratch it.

choices.consequence: You produce the smile of quiet optimism and hold it the full eight minutes, and she singles you out by name for praise, and the relief makes you feel sick.
You keep your face empty, which is safer than wrong, and which is also, technically, an expression they have printed a form for.

nodes.text: She works in Fiction, on the novel-writing machines, and wears the scarlet sash of the Junior Anti-Sex League cinched tight over her overalls. You have hated her on sight for a year, because that grade of purity is usually an informer. In the corridor she trips against a wall and you help her up, and there is a folded scrap left in your palm. Three words. Not a denunciation. Worse than one.

choices.consequence: You believe it on no evidence whatsoever, because the alternative is a life with nothing at all in it, and because the handwriting is round and hurried.
You assume a trap for six days and take lunch alone in the corner, and read the note every night regardless, which rather settles the question.

nodes.text: An hour on two trains and then a walk, out to a hollow of grass where bluebells have come up because nobody has yet found a reason to concrete it. She checks for microphones by shaking a branch and listening. No screens anywhere. Her mouth tastes of the saccharine tablets everyone chews. When she takes the sash off you understand that it was camouflage, and always had been.

choices.consequence: You let the afternoon simply be an afternoon — sun, grass, a thrush going on about nothing for ten minutes — and afterwards cannot account for the time, which is the point of it.
You watch the treeline the entire hour and count the exits twice, and she notices, and says nothing, and something small between you is spent.

nodes.text: Above the junk shop in the prole quarter: a bed with bugs in it, a print of a church nobody living remembers, and a glass paperweight with a scrap of coral set inside like something caught in amber. Four dollars. No telescreen at all — Charrington says they never bothered installing one, too expensive. The rent is a month of your salary and the rest of your neck.

choices.consequence: You take it, and for four months you have a bed and a woman who brings real coffee up the stairs, and you both know precisely what you are spending on it.
You say no, twice, and go back a fortnight later with the money already counted in your pocket, which means the decision was never actually taken.

nodes.text: Syme, two desks down, is compiling the next Newspeak dictionary and is delighted about it. The point, he explains over the canteen stew, is destruction: cut 'excellent' and 'splendid', keep 'plusgood', and by 2050 no head anywhere will be able to hold the sentence you wrote in your diary. He is far too intelligent about it. He will be vapourised inside the year.

choices.consequence: You note it privately — that they are not censoring the thought so much as demolishing the housing it lives in — and it goes into the diary that night.
You agree with Syme enthusiastically and steer him back to the chess problem, and he looks at you with the mild contempt of a man who won't survive his own cleverness.

nodes.text: The rectification arrives through the pneumatic tube: Comrade Withers, formerly of the Inner Party, unperson. You write him a replacement — Comrade Ogilvy, who never lived, who joined the Spies at six and died heroically at twenty-three — and file it in the proper style. Withers goes down the memory hole in the wall, into the furnaces below the building, and has therefore never existed.

choices.consequence: You spend the afternoon wondering whether Ogilvy is now more real than Withers, and conclude, correctly, that in every way that can be checked he is.
You clear the tray, take the tea break, and get through the rest of the shift without once thinking about it. That is a skill you have been building for years.

nodes.text: O'Brien is Inner Party: black overalls, a prizefighter's face, and the manners of a man who has read books he is permitted to read. He stops you in the corridor about the new dictionary and mentions Syme's name in the past tense without breaking stride. Then he offers his address, for an advance copy, and holds your eye half a second past what the errand requires.

choices.consequence: You go, with Julia, up in a lift that actually works, into a flat where the telescreen can be switched off — and he switches it off, and the silence nearly stops your heart.
You put it off three weeks and the address stays folded in your pocket, and you take it out and look at it the way a man looks at a bottle he has promised to leave alone.

nodes.text: It comes in brown paper: heavy, badly bound, no author's name on it anywhere — the Brotherhood's book, the thing every child in Oceania is taught to be frightened of. In the attic, with Julia's head on your arm and the prole woman singing at her washing line under the window, you read the chapter on why the war must never end. It explains everything and tells you nothing you did not already know.

choices.consequence: You read it aloud to her and she is asleep by the second page, and you keep going anyway, and the happiest hour of your life is spent on political theory.
You put it under the loose board and lie awake calculating how long it would take them to find it, and settle on about four minutes.

nodes.text: Charrington had grey in his hair and the thickened vowels of the prole quarter, and sold you the coral for four dollars, and taught you the next line of the rhyme about the bells. Later — much, much too late — you will remember he wore glasses, and that his face belonged to a man of sixty, and that the Thought Police have been running that shop for longer than you have been alive.

choices.consequence: Something in the way he pronounces the old rhyme sits wrong, and you put it aside, because the alternative is that the room was never yours at any point.
You go on liking him — the snuffbox, the prints, the shop-smell of dust and mice — and buy the paperweight's twin for Julia, and thank him for the loan of a life.

nodes.text: A voice comes out of the wall behind the church print and pleasantly recites the last line of the rhyme back at you. Then boots on the stairs, a great many of them, unhurried. Somebody puts a fist into Julia's stomach and she folds up like a carpenter's rule. A man knocks the paperweight off the table and it breaks, and what astonishes you is how small the piece of coral actually is.

choices.consequence: You stand very still with your hands where they can be seen, and it alters nothing whatsoever about what follows, and you knew that before you did it.
You get one arm loose and swing at nobody, and they let you, and then a boot finds your elbow and the fight goes out of you for a year.

nodes.text: There are no windows and the lights are never turned off, so time comes apart in your hands. Four days, possibly nine. The ordinary guards break your teeth first with truncheons, and that part is nearly restful because it asks nothing of you. Then the questioning. They have the diary. They have every word of it and every date, and nobody in the room is angry.

choices.consequence: You hold her name behind your teeth through all of it, and O'Brien tells you kindly that they already have everything she has said, and that he is not asking for information.
You give her up on the second day, in detail, with dates, and it changes nothing at all, because the confession was never the object of the exercise.

nodes.text: O'Brien explains it without drama: the worst thing in the world, which is a different thing for each person, and which they have known about you since before you bought the diary. The cage has two compartments and a mask shaped to fit a face. The rats are large and grey and the colour of old bread, and they have not been fed, and there is a door between.

choices.consequence: You hold for one second and then two, and your entire life narrows to a length of wire being drawn slowly back, and nothing else exists anywhere.
You beg — for the world, for anything, for the mask off — and hear your own voice climb into a register you did not know it had.

nodes.text: You scream it at the ceiling before you have decided to. Do it to Julia. Not me. Put her face in it, put it on her, do it to Julia. And it is not a lie told to stop the wire. It is an actual wish, warm and complete, and it lasts perhaps a second and a half, and a second and a half is the entire requirement. The mask comes away.

choices.consequence: You meant it, and you know you meant it, and that knowledge is the product they were manufacturing the whole time.
You tell yourself afterwards that you did not mean it, and rehearse the argument nightly, and it holds up a little less well every year.

nodes.text: They release you: teeth replaced, a post on a sub-committee that convenes to decide nothing, more money than you earned before. Victory Square, the Chestnut Tree Café, a corner table nobody else takes. The gin arrives at any hour without being asked for. It smells of cloves and tastes of nitric acid, and it is now the flavour of most of your waking life.

choices.consequence: You are drinking before noon without having noticed you started, and the waiter fills it again unprompted, and the afternoon goes down easily enough.
You leave the glass standing a full minute as a sort of test, and then drink it, and the result of the test is recorded nowhere but in you.

nodes.text: March, in the park, wind bending the bare trees. She is thicker at the waist and there is a long scar across her forehead that you do not ask about, and her body has gone stiff, as though there were wire under it. 'I betrayed you,' she says, in the tone of someone reporting the weather. You say you betrayed her. After that there is nothing left that needs saying.

choices.consequence: You walk off toward the tube without looking back, and are relieved, which is the very last thing you would have predicted a year ago.
You sit on the bench a while longer beside a woman you no longer want, out of manners you cannot name, and the cold gets thoroughly into both of you.

nodes.text: The chess problem runs in the paper every week: white to play and mate in two. You lay it out with the café's greasy pieces, solve it, and set it up again. White always wins. Always, in every problem they have ever printed, without a single exception, because somebody a long time ago decided that was the correct arrangement of a board.

choices.consequence: You move the bishop and see the mate land three seconds before it does, and the small clean pleasure of it is the only pleasure left that has no gin in it.
You push the board away and watch the screen instead, because solving things is a habit belonging to the man you used to be.

nodes.text: The bulletin cuts across the music: the Eurasian armies in Central Africa annihilated, half a million prisoners taken, the entire southern front collapsed. The café goes up in noise around you. Something lifts in your chest on cue and the tears come, and you cannot tell whether they belong to the victory, or to the gin, or simply to the general problem of arranging your face.

choices.consequence: You cheer along with the room and mean it entirely for as long as the cheer lasts, and the warmth of belonging is real, and you had forgotten it was available.
You sit still through the whole of it, and nobody notices, because there is no longer anything in you worth anyone's watching for.

nodes.text: The rhyme surfaces from somewhere: oranges and lemons, say the bells of St Clement's. Charrington taught you the line that follows. There was a woman in the yard beneath the attic window who sang the whole of it at her washing, with pegs in her mouth, and the fact that this happened is still, technically, filed somewhere in your head alongside the coral and the grass.

choices.consequence: You hum four bars into the gin glass and a man at the next table glances up, and you stop, and the tune goes on inside where they cannot reach it. For now.
You cut it off mid-bar deliberately, because a tune is a door, and you have made a very careful decision about doors.

nodes.text: The face fills the screen: black-moustached, calm, looking at you and at nobody else in the room. Forty years you have been in the same building as that face. Something happens in your chest for which you have no word except the obvious one, and the obvious one is correct, and it is quiet and enormous and has evidently been waiting for you the entire time.

choices.consequence: You watch it happen from a small distance, the way a man studies his own X-ray, and note that it is love and that nobody is forcing it.
You push back against it for the length of one held breath and find nothing behind the push — no argument, no Julia, no diary, only the wall where those were.

nodes.text: There is a stationer's on the way to the café with pads in the window, poor grey paper, the sort nobody bothers to ration. You stop outside it for as long as it takes a bus to go past. The thought arrives complete and mild, the way weather arrives: you could buy paper. Then the bus is gone and the window is only a window with pads in it.

choices.consequence: You walk on, and the thought does not return, and its not returning is the last thing to happen to you that would have interested anybody.
You go in and buy two pads and a pencil with a soft lead, pay in coins, and do not ask yourself why until you are already home with the door shut.
You keep walking past the shop and past the café and down to the tube, and buy a ticket to a station near a field you visited once.

nodes.text: The rest of it is a great many afternoons at the same table, and gin, and the correct feelings arriving punctually. The sub-committee decides nothing and you never once mind. When you die — pneumonia, a wet winter, no diary anywhere — the last things in your head are a bulletin from the southern front and a tune you have always liked, and everything that was in you before has been removed cleanly, as though rectified. Which it was.

You buy the pads. You write in the small hours in the corner the screen cannot quite reach: the field, the thrush, the coral, her scar, the wire, and what you shouted at the ceiling. No slogans and no arguments — only what happened, what it cost, and who you were before it. You wrap the lot in oilcloth and put it under a flagstone in a yard. Two centuries on, a young scholar sits with it in cotton gloves, cannot find your name anywhere in it, and keeps looking.

On the worst nights, when the gin isn't working, you go back to the hollow with the bluebells in it. The train, the walk, the sash lying on the grass, one hour in which nobody was watching and nothing had to be performed. They took everything else. They did not get that, because you never wrote it down and never said it aloud, not once, not even to her. You decide the hour was worth the whole of the rest. You tell nobody. That is the point.
